description: How fair play, team spirit, citizenship, national pride and excellence shape sport.
content_html:
Why Values Matter in Sport

Sport can teach people far more than a skill or a technique. At its best, sport builds character: it demands that we co-operate with teammates, accept decisions from officials, respect opponents, and push ourselves beyond our comfort zone. These qualities are not accidental — they are sporting values: the principles that sport promotes and that participants are expected to show. The specification identifies seven distinct values. Learning them by name and being able to apply each to a specific sporting context is a core exam skill.

Key Fact

The seven sporting values are: team spirit, fair play, citizenship, tolerance and respect (counted as one value in the specification), inclusion, national pride, and excellence. Learn all seven — examiners will penalise answers that miss one or conflate them.

Team Spirit

Team spirit is the collective sense of belonging and mutual support that develops when a group of athletes work toward a shared goal. It is visible when a rugby player sets the ball back for a teammate rather than taking the credit themselves, or when a swimming relay team celebrates every individual's split time as equally important. Team spirit is not just about winning together — it is about maintaining morale during defeat, supporting injured players, and trusting the collective even when individual form is poor. Research consistently shows that teams with strong team spirit outperform their expected ability level in high-pressure situations.

Fair Play

Fair play means playing within both the written rules and the unwritten spirit of a sport. It includes acknowledging good play by an opponent, accepting a referee’s decision without argument, and not seeking an unfair advantage through cheating, gamesmanship or simulation. In football, kicking the ball out of play voluntarily when an opponent is injured — and then returning it when play restarts — is a well-known example of fair play that is not written in the laws of the game but is universally expected. Governing bodies such as The FA and the International Olympic Committee run specific fair play awards to recognise and publicise examples of this value.

Citizenship in sport describes how athletes, clubs and governing bodies contribute positively to the wider community. It goes beyond sport itself: a professional footballer visiting a children’s hospital, a local rugby club providing free sessions to young people at risk of exclusion, or athletes campaigning for environmental sustainability at major events are all examples. Citizenship recognises that elite athletes have a platform and a responsibility to use it for social good.

In school sport, citizenship shows when a team captain encourages a younger student to try the sport, or when athletes volunteer to help at a community event. The value is not just for elite sport — it applies at every level from grassroots to international.

Tolerance and Respect

The specification treats tolerance and respect as a single value. Tolerance means accepting that other people have different backgrounds, beliefs, abilities and approaches to sport. Respect means actively valuing others — opponents, officials, spectators and teammates — regardless of those differences. In practice, this looks like: applauding an opponent’s excellent performance, not arguing with a referee’s call, welcoming athletes from different cultural backgrounds without prejudice, and adapting language and behaviour to make everyone feel included. The Premier League’s “No Room For Racism” campaign is one example of how professional sport institutionalises this value.

Key Fact

Tolerance and respect are listed as a single value — not two separate ones. Older textbooks sometimes split them. The specification wording is ‘tolerance and respect’ as a paired phrase. Always write them together.

Inclusion

Inclusion means ensuring that sport is accessible and welcoming to everyone, regardless of age, gender, disability, ethnicity or socio-economic background. It overlaps with removing barriers but is a value rather than a policy: it describes the attitude sports organisations and participants should hold. Disability sport is one of the clearest expressions of inclusion — the Paralympic movement insists that people with disabilities should have equal opportunities to compete at the highest level, not just take part in modified recreational activities. Inclusion also means mixed-ability sessions, disability-friendly coaching qualifications, and communication in accessible formats.

National Pride

Sport creates one of the most powerful settings for national pride: representing your country at international level, hearing your national anthem before a match, or seeing your flag raised on a medal podium. National pride brings communities together across social divides — for a few weeks during a major tournament, people who would otherwise have little in common find shared identity through their national team. The 2024 Paris Olympics generated significant national pride across the UK, with athletes from diverse backgrounds becoming symbols of national achievement. Research suggests that hosting or succeeding in major sporting events increases public wellbeing beyond the sporting community itself.

Excellence

Excellence in sport is the pursuit of being the very best you can be — not necessarily winning, but striving consistently to improve performance, training habits and competitive standards. The Olympic motto “Citius, Altius, Fortius — Communiter” (Faster, Higher, Stronger — Together) captures this value: the aspiration to continually reach beyond current limits. Excellence is visible in an athlete who trains at 6 am daily, in a club that invests in professional coaching, and in a young performer who asks for feedback and works on their weaknesses rather than coasting on natural ability.

The most common mistake in values questions is vague or circular answers. Writing “fair play means playing fairly” earns no marks. You must name the value, define it precisely, and then anchor it to a specific sporting example. For example: “Fair play is playing within both the rules and the spirit of the sport. An example is a tennis player who calls a ball ‘out’ on their own side, overruling their advantage, because they saw it land in.” The examiner wants definition + applied example. Write both, every time.

Also remember that ‘evaluate’ questions about values ask you to weigh how far sport actually promotes the value — not just to describe what the value is. Real sport also contains examples of values being violated (doping, racism, simulation). A strong evaluative answer acknowledges both sides.
exam_tip_html: For ‘evaluate’ questions about sporting values, you must argue both sides — examples where sport promotes the value AND examples where the value is violated. A one-sided answer that only shows sport at its best will not reach the top mark band. Always include a specific sporting example to support each point, and end with a justified judgement stating how far you agree overall. Vague statements like ‘sport teaches people to respect each other’ without an example will not score highly — examiners reward applied answers.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The seven sporting values are team spirit, fair play, citizenship, tolerance and respect (one value), inclusion, national pride, and excellence — learn all seven with one example each.
  • Tolerance and respect are treated as a single paired value in the specification — do not split them into two separate values.
  • For evaluation questions, sport can both promote and violate values — you need examples of both sides plus a final judgement to reach the highest mark band.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a sporting value as defined in the specification?
A) Competitiveness
B) Aggression
C) Excellence
D) Determination
State two sporting values that relate to how athletes treat others on and off the field of play.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: fair play / tolerance and respect / citizenship / inclusion. (Accept any two genuine and distinct answers. 'Team spirit' focuses on internal group cohesion rather than treatment of others so should be marked with care — credit if the student explains it in terms of mutual support.) [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by the sporting value of 'citizenship' and give one example from sport.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 3 marks. 1 mark for a basic definition ('citizenship is about giving back to the wider community'). 2 marks for a developed definition ('citizenship means athletes and clubs using their platform and skills to contribute positively to society beyond sport'). 3 marks for adding a specific example ('for example, a Premier League club that runs free football sessions in a deprived area to reduce youth crime is demonstrating citizenship by using sport as a tool for social good'). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the sporting value of 'national pride' and give one example of how it is expressed in a major sporting event.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (up to 2 marks): national pride is a sense of pride in one's country that is expressed through supporting national teams and athletes; sport provides a setting where people from different backgrounds find shared identity through representing or cheering for their nation (2 marks for a developed description; 1 mark for a basic statement).
Example (up to 2 marks): at the 2024 Paris Olympics, athletes across many sports competed under the British flag; hearing the national anthem at a medal ceremony and seeing athletes from diverse backgrounds celebrated as national heroes both expressed and created national pride among millions of viewers (2 marks for a specific, applied example; 1 mark for a vague reference). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
Westbourne Harriers is a community athletics club. A group of parents have complained that the club cares only about winning and that younger, less able athletes are being made to feel unwelcome. The club coach argues that pursuing excellence is the most important value in sport.

Discuss whether excellence should be the priority in a community sports club, or whether other values should take precedence.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A developed discussion that presents both sides clearly. Arguments for excellence as priority: high standards attract better athletes, produce results, and create role models; athletes who do not strive to improve may undermine the competitive culture of the club. Arguments for other values taking priority: inclusion and team spirit ensure all ability levels feel welcome; a community club has a social responsibility beyond results; fair play and citizenship matter to the club's reputation and its links with local schools. The answer considers more than one perspective and may reach a justified view.
Secure (3–4 marks): Both sides identified with some development, but balance may be uneven.
Developing (2 marks): One side only, or two points without development.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Bridgewater FC is a semi-professional women's football club in a medium-sized UK town. Over the past season, the club has experienced two serious incidents: one player received racial abuse from opposing supporters, and a match was abandoned after a brawl involving players from both teams.

Evaluate how far sport genuinely promotes the values of tolerance and respect and fair play, using the scenario above and your own sporting knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): A balanced evaluation that uses the Bridgewater FC scenario alongside broader knowledge. Arguments that sport promotes these values: governing bodies mandate fair play codes, referees enforce rules punishing disrespect (yellow cards, bans), campaigns like No Room For Racism actively tackle discrimination, and many athletes model exemplary behaviour on and off the pitch. Arguments that sport fails to promote these values: the two incidents at Bridgewater FC show that rules and campaigns have not eliminated abuse or violence; research suggests gamesmanship (time-wasting, simulation) is widespread at elite level; media coverage of poor conduct may normalise it. A substantiated judgement concludes how far sport promotes these values overall — for example, 'sport provides the framework for these values but cannot guarantee them; the behaviour of participants ultimately depends on individual character and club culture.' No judgement = cannot reach Mastering.
Secure (5–6 marks): Both sides developed with the scenario and broader examples; judgement present but may be thin.
Developing (3–4 marks): Points made but one-sided or judgement missing.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic points with no evaluation. [8 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: How many sporting values are listed in the specification?
The specification treats which two concepts as a single paired sporting value?
Kicking the ball out of play voluntarily when an opponent is injured, and returning it when play restarts, is a well-known example of _____.
The value that describes how athletes and clubs contribute positively to their wider community beyond sport is called _____.
Match each sporting value to the correct description.
right: Ensuring sport is accessible to everyone regardless of background
A sense of pride in one's country through sporting achievement
Striving consistently to be the very best you can be

flashcard_questions.q: How many sporting values are named in the specification?
What is the correct specification term that combines two concepts into a single sporting value?
What is team spirit in sport?
flashcard_questions.a: A sense of unity and mutual support within a group working toward a shared goal.

flashcard_questions.q: What does fair play mean beyond following the written rules?
flashcard_questions.a: Playing within the spirit of the sport and not seeking an unfair advantage.

flashcard_questions.q: What does citizenship in sport describe an athlete contributing to?
flashcard_questions.a: The wider community beyond their sport.

flashcard_questions.q: What value does a football player show by voluntarily kicking the ball out for an injured opponent?
Which sporting value means ensuring that everyone can participate, regardless of disability or background?
What value is expressed when athletes represent their country and hear their national anthem at a medal ceremony?
What is 'excellence' as a sporting value?
flashcard_questions.a: The pursuit of being the best you can be through consistent effort and improvement.

flashcard_questions.q: What single value does the Olympic motto 'Citius, Altius, Fortius' express?
What is the key difference between defining a sporting value and demonstrating it in an exam answer?
flashcard_questions.a: An exam answer must include both a definition and a specific sporting example.

flashcard_questions.q: Name one campaign that demonstrates the value of tolerance and respect in professional football.

glossary_terms.definition: Principles or standards of behaviour that sport promotes and that participants are expected to demonstrate.
A sense of unity, mutual support and shared purpose within a group of athletes working toward a common goal.
The contribution of athletes and sports clubs to the wider community, demonstrating responsibility toward others beyond sport itself.
A sense of pride in one's country expressed through supporting national teams and athletes in sport.

items.title: Legendary Respect and Fair Play Moments in Sports
items.description: Compilation of iconic sportsmanship moments — athletes helping injured opponents, withdrawing advantages, and applauding rivals — perfect applied examples for fair play and tolerance and respect answers.

items.title: Most Beautiful Moments of Respect and Fair Play in Sports
items.description: Further compilation including cricket, athletics and football moments that show what sportsmanship looks like in practice across different sports.

items.title: 100% Sportsmanship Moments in Sports History
items.description: Athletes choosing character over results — excellent source of specific sporting examples you can quote in an evaluate question about whether sport genuinely promotes its values.

items.title: Chariots of Fire (1981)
items.description: Two British runners at the 1924 Paris Olympics — a film about national pride, personal values, and what it means to compete for your country while staying true to your principles.

items.title: Cool Runnings (1993)
items.description: The Jamaican bobsled team earns the respect of rivals through determination and fair play — a crowd-pleasing study in team spirit and national pride against the odds.

items.title: Sport England — Values in Sport
items.description: Sport England's overview of what sporting values mean at grassroots level and how clubs are encouraged to embed them — useful real-world context beyond elite sport.

items.title: Premier League — No Room For Racism Campaign
items.description: Detail on how professional football institutionalises the value of tolerance and respect through a coordinated anti-racism programme — a specific campaign example for exam answers.

items.title: BBC Sport — Fair Play in Football: The Unwritten Rules
items.description: Feature on the conventions of fair play in football — returning the ball after an injury stoppage, not exploiting a goalkeeper's injury — with examples from recent seasons.

items.title: Women in Sport — Inclusion in Sport
items.description: Research and case studies on what inclusion looks like in practice across different sports — relevant for evaluate questions on whether sport genuinely promotes inclusion.
